proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(t=m/n\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:aspect\mbox{-}ratio}\) gives \(t\in[c_-,c_+]\).  Choose \(c_0<1\).  On the regime \(b_{nm}\le c_0\), the truncation in \(\mathrm{def:frontier\mbox{-}rate}\) is inactive, and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{nm}
&=\frac{B}{\lambda_{nm}}K r^{3/2}\mu q^{-1/2}
  \sqrt{\log(en)}\sqrt{nm}\sqrt{n^{-1}+nm^{-2}}\\
&=K r^{3/2}\mu\sqrt{t+t^{-1}}
  \frac{B}{\lambda_{nm}}\sqrt{\frac{n\log(en)}q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, for
\[
s_{nm}:=\frac{B}{\lambda_{nm}}\sqrt{\frac{n\log(en)}q},
\]
there are constants \(C_-,C_+>0\), depending only on \(r,K,\mu,c_-,c_+\), such that
\[
C_-s_{nm}\le b_{nm}\le C_+s_{nm}.
\tag{1}
\]

We construct a constant-propensity subexperiment.  Since \(r\) is fixed, partition \(I\) into disjoint balanced blocks \(I_1,\ldots,I_r\) and \(J\) into disjoint balanced blocks \(J_1,\ldots,J_r\); their sizes differ by at most one.  Write \(N_s=|I_s|\) and \(M_s=|J_s|\).  For \(s\ge2\), let \(u_s=N_s^{-1/2}{\bf1}_{I_s}\), viewed in \(\mathbb R^n\), and for every \(s\) let \(v_s=M_s^{-1/2}{\bf1}_{J_s}\), viewed in \(\mathbb R^m\).  Put \(u_0=N_1^{-1/2}{\bf1}_{I_1}\), fix \(k_0\in I_1\), and, for \(k\in\mathcal K:=I_1\setminus\{k_0\}\), define
\[
w_k=\frac{e_k-e_{k_0}}{\sqrt2},\qquad
\delta=a\frac{B}{\lambda_{nm}}\sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}q},\qquad
u_k=\frac{u_0+\delta w_k}{\sqrt{1+\delta^2}},
\tag{2}
\]
where \(a>0\) is fixed below.  The vectors \(u_0\) and \(w_k\) are orthogonal unit vectors, so \(u_k\) is a unit vector.  Disjoint block supports give
\[
U_k=(u_k,u_2,\ldots,u_r)\in\mathbb O_{n,r},
\qquad V=(v_1,\ldots,v_r)\in\mathbb O_{m,r}.
\]
Set \(U_0=(u_0,u_2,\ldots,u_r)\) and
\[
M_k=\lambda_{nm}U_kV^\top\quad(k\in\mathcal K),
\qquad M_0=\lambda_{nm}U_0V^\top.
\tag{3}
\]

We verify all model restrictions.  Equations (1)--(2) imply
\[
\delta\sqrt n=a s_{nm}\le aC_-^{-1}b_{nm}\le aC_-^{-1}c_0.
\tag{4}
\]
For a row in \(I_1\), the triangle inequality gives
\[
\lVert e_i^\top U_k\rVert_2\le N_1^{-1/2}+\delta/\sqrt2.
\tag{5}
\]
For a row in \(I_s\), \(s\ge2\), its row norm is \(N_s^{-1/2}\).  Balanced blocks and fixed \(r\) give \(\max_s\sqrt{n/N_s}\to\sqrt r\).  The strict inequality \(\mu>1\) supplies positive slack between \(\sqrt r\) and \(\sqrt{\mu r}\).  First choose \(ac_0\) small enough relative to that slack and the constants in (4), and then take \(n\) sufficiently large.  Equations (4)--(5) yield
\[
\lVert U_k\rVert_{2,\infty}\le\sqrt{\mu r/n}.
\tag{6}
\]
The same balanced-block calculation, without a perturbation, gives
\[
\lVert V\rVert_{2,\infty}\le\sqrt{\mu r/m}
\tag{7}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(m\).  Thus (6)--(7) verify the two incoherence assumptions.  By (3), every nonzero singular value of \(M_k\) equals \(\lambda_{nm}\).  Hence exact rank, the signal floor, and the condition-number bound hold; the last uses \(K\ge1\).

For all sufficiently large dimensions, balanced blocks satisfy \(N_s\ge n/(2r)\) and \(M_s\ge m/(2r)\).  Equations (2)--(3) then imply
\[
\max_{i,j}|(M_k)_{ij}|
\le \frac{2r\lambda_{nm}}{\sqrt{nm}}
   +aB\sqrt{\frac{2r\log(en)}{qm}}.
\tag{8}
\]
Choose \(c_1>0\) so that \(2rc_1\le1/4\).  Under \(\lambda_{nm}\le c_1B\sqrt{nm}\), the first term in (8) is at most \(B/4\).  The second is at most \(B/4\) for all sufficiently large \(n,m\), by fixed \(q,r,a\) and bounded aspect ratio.  Consequently
\[
\max_{i,j}|(M_k)_{ij}|\le B/2
\tag{9}
\]
uniformly in \(k\in\mathcal K\cup\{0\}\).

For each such \(k\), define a law \(P_k\) as follows.  Set \(Y_{ij}(0)=0\).  Independently across cells, draw \(Y_{ij}(1)\in\{-B,B\}\) with
\[
P_k\{Y_{ij}(1)=B\}
=h_{k,ij}:=\frac12\left(1+\frac{(M_k)_{ij}}B\right).
\tag{10}
\]
Independently of all potential outcomes and across cells, draw \(A_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\), and record \(p_{ij}=q\).  Equation (9) puts every \(h_{k,ij}\) in \([1/4,3/4]\), while (10) gives \(E_{P_k}[Y_{ij}(1)]=(M_k)_{ij}\).  Independence from all earlier cells in the filtration \(\mathrm{def:global\mbox{-}filtration}\) gives
\[
\mu^1_{ij}=E_{P_k}[Y_{ij}(1)\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}]=(M_k)_{ij},
\qquad \mu^0_{ij}=0.
\tag{11}
\]
Thus the causal matrix \(M=\mu^1-\mu^0\) equals \(M_k\); it has not been defined through the observed score.  Independence of \(A_{ij}\) from the potential outcomes, also conditionally on the recorded past, verifies sequential randomization.  The equality \(p_{ij}=q\), with \(q<1/2\), verifies overlap.  The support in (10) and \(Y_{ij}(0)=0\) verify bounded outcomes.  Equations (6)--(7), the singular-value calculation, and the assumed dimension path verify every other member condition.  Hence
\[
P_k\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}(r,\mu,K,q,B,\lambda)
\quad(k\in\mathcal K\cup\{0\}).
\tag{12}
\]

We next bound information in \(\mathcal O_{n,m}=\sigma(A,Y,p)\).  If \(x,y\in[-B/2,B/2]\), put \(s=(1+x/B)/2\) and \(t'=(1+y/B)/2\).  For fixed \(t'\in[1/4,3/4]\), the Bernoulli relative entropy \(f(s)=s\log(s/t')+(1-s)\log((1-s)/(1-t'))\) satisfies
\[
f(t')=f'(t')=0,
\qquad f''(s)=\frac1{s(1-s)}\le\frac{16}3.
\]
Taylor's theorem therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{kl}\left(\frac{1+x/B}{2},\frac{1+y/B}{2}\right)
\le\frac{2}{3}\frac{(x-y)^2}{B^2}.
\tag{13}
\]
The assignment law and recorded propensity are identical under \(P_k\) and \(P_0\).  Given \(A_{ij}=0\), the observed outcome has the common value zero; given \(A_{ij}=1\), its sign has Bernoulli parameter \(h_{k,ij}\).  Independence across cells, (13), and direct factorization of the observed likelihood give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{KL}(P_k^{\mathcal O},P_0^{\mathcal O})
&=q\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{kl}(h_{k,ij},h_{0,ij})\\
&\le\frac{Cq}{B^2}\lVert M_k-M_0\rVert_F^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
Only the first singular component differs in (3), and \(\lVert v_1\rVert_2=1\), so
\[
\lVert M_k-M_0\rVert_F^2
=\lambda_{nm}^2\lVert u_k-u_0\rVert_2^2.
\]
Orthogonality in (2) gives
\[
\lVert u_k-u_0\rVert_2^2
=2\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt{1+\delta^2}}\right)\le\delta^2.
\]
Substitution into (14) proves
\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_k^{\mathcal O},P_0^{\mathcal O})
\le Ca^2\log(en).
\tag{15}
\]

The alternatives are separated in the declared rowwise loss.  For distinct \(k,\ell\in\mathcal K\), inspect row \(k\).  Only the first columns of \(U_k\) and \(U_\ell\) can be nonzero on that row, and (2) gives
\[
\lVert e_k^\top U_k\rVert_2-\lVert e_k^\top U_\ell\rVert_2
=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{2(1+\delta^2)}}.
\]
Right multiplication by any \(R\in\mathbb O_r\) preserves row norms.  The reverse triangle inequality thus gives
\[
\min_{R\in\mathbb O_r}\lVert U_kR-U_\ell\rVert_{2,\infty}
\ge\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{2(1+\delta^2)}}.
\]
By \(\mathrm{def:rowwise\mbox{-}loss}\),
\[
\mathcal L(U_k,U_\ell)
\ge\Delta_{nm}:=\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}
\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{2(1+\delta^2)}}.
\tag{16}
\]
Equation (4) makes \(\delta\le1\) eventually.  Combining (1), (2), and (16), uniformly for \(t\in[c_-,c_+]\), gives a constant \(c>0\) such that
\[
\Delta_{nm}\ge cb_{nm}.
\tag{17}
\]
Indeed, before the bounded factor \(1/\sqrt{2(1+\delta^2)}\), the exact ratio is
\[
\frac{\sqrt{n/(\mu r)}\,\delta}{b_{nm}}
=\frac{a}{K r^2\mu^{3/2}\sqrt{t+t^{-1}}}.
\]

For completeness, we derive the multiple-testing reduction.  Let \(D=|\mathcal K|=N_1-1\), let \(\Theta\) be uniform on \(\mathcal K\), and conditionally on \(\Theta=k\) draw the observed experiment from \(P_k^{\mathcal O}\).  With \(\overline P=D^{-1}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}P_k^{\mathcal O}\), expansion of the logarithms yields
\[
I(\Theta;\mathcal O)
=\frac1D\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\operatorname{KL}(P_k^{\mathcal O},P_0^{\mathcal O})
-\operatorname{KL}(\overline P,P_0^{\mathcal O}).
\]
Nonnegativity of relative entropy and (15) imply
\[
I(\Theta;\mathcal O)\le Ca^2\log(en).
\tag{18}
\]
For any decoder \(\widehat\Theta\), put \(P_e=P(\widehat\Theta\ne\Theta)\).  Conditioning the entropy of \(\Theta\) on the error indicator gives
\[
H(\Theta\mid\mathcal O)\le\log2+P_e\log D.
\]
Since \(H(\Theta)=\log D\), (18) gives
\[
P_e\ge1-\frac{Ca^2\log(en)+\log2}{\log D}.
\tag{19}
\]
Balanced blocks give \(D\asymp n\).  Choose \(a>0\) sufficiently small, depending only on the fixed theorem quantities, so the right side of (19) is at least \(1/2\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).

Finally take \(\widetilde U\in\mathfrak E_{n,m}\) and decode by a nearest member of \(\{U_k:k\in\mathcal K\}\) in the orthogonal-quotient \(2,\infty\) distance.  That distance obeys the triangle inequality: compose two orthogonal alignments and use invariance of row norms under right orthogonal multiplication.  Therefore a decoding error under \(P_k\), pairwise separation (16), and nearest-neighbor decoding imply
\[
\mathcal L(\widetilde U,U_k)\ge\Delta_{nm}/2.
\]
Averaging over the uniform index, then using (19) and (17), gives
\[
\sup_{k\in\mathcal K}E_{P_k}[\mathcal L(\widetilde U,U_k)]
\ge\frac{\Delta_{nm}}4\ge c_2b_{nm}.
\]
By (12), the finite family is a subset of the frozen predictable class and has \(p_{ij}=q\) at every cell.  Taking the supremum over the class and then the infimum over \(\widetilde U\in\mathfrak E_{n,m}\) proves the theorem.

Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:ipw\mbox{-}expected\mbox{-}risk\mbox{-}upper}\) gives
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}}
E_P[\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm I},U)]
\le C a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}.
\]
The radius is strictly positive because \(B,q,\lambda_{nm}>0\) and \(n,m\ge2\).  Markov's inequality consequently gives, for every \(t>0\),
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}}
P\{\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm I},U)>t a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}\}
\le C/t,
\]
which is the asserted uniform \(O_P(a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm})\) statement.  Neither the definition nor the proof of this radius involves \(\mathcal G_n\), so it has no query-family factor.

For the last assertion, \(\mathrm{prop:adaptive\mbox{-}endogenous\mbox{-}target\mbox{-}obstruction}\) supplies a sequence \(P_n\) in the same class and constants \(c_0,c_1>0\) such that \(b_{nn}\to0\) and
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}P_n\{\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm I},U)>c_0\}\ge c_1.
\]
If recorded IPW--SVD were uniformly \(O_P(b_{nm})\), then for \(\varepsilon=c_1/2\) a finite \(T\) would make the probability at threshold \(Tb_{nn}\) at most \(\varepsilon\) eventually.  Since \(Tb_{nn}<c_0\) eventually, this contradicts the preceding display.  The witness evaluates only \(\widehat U^{\mathrm I}\), so it proves no impossibility claim for any other estimator.

Fix \(P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}(r,\mu,K,q,B,\lambda)\), and expose cells in the row-major order of \(\mathrm{def:global\mbox{-}filtration}\).  By \(\mathrm{lem:ipw\mbox{-}identification}\),
\[
E_P[E_{ij}\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}]=0.
\tag{20}
\]
Sequential randomization, overlap, and bounded outcomes give
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_P[(Z^{\mathrm{ipw}}_{ij})^2\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}]
&=E_P\!\left[
\frac{Y_{ij}(1)^2}{p_{ij}}+
\frac{Y_{ij}(0)^2}{1-p_{ij}}
\mathrel{\Big|}\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}\right]\\
&\le\frac{2B^2}{q}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
\]
For the equality, condition first on the two potential outcomes and use \(P(A_{ij}=1\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1},Y_{ij}(0),Y_{ij}(1))=p_{ij}\); both divisions are valid by overlap.  Since \(M_{ij}=E_P[Z^{\mathrm{ipw}}_{ij}\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}]\), conditional variance is no larger than (21).  Also \(|Z^{\mathrm{ipw}}_{ij}|\le B/q\), while bounded outcomes and conditional Jensen give \(|M_{ij}|\le2B\).  Since \(q<1/2\),
\[
|E_{ij}|\le\frac{2B}{q}.
\tag{22}
\]

Introduce the self-adjoint dilation
\[
\Delta_{ij}=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&E_{ij}e_ie_j^\top\\
E_{ij}e_je_i^\top&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Equation (20) makes these matrix martingale differences.  Their norms equal \(|E_{ij}|\), and their squares have diagonal blocks \(E_{ij}^2e_ie_i^\top\) and \(E_{ij}^2e_je_j^\top\).  Hence (21) gives the deterministic predictable-variation bound
\[
\left\lVert\sum_{i,j}E_P[\Delta_{ij}^2\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}]\right\rVert
\le v_{nm}:=\frac{2B^2(n\vee m)}q.
\tag{23}
\]
Apply \(\mathrm{lem:tropp\mbox{-}matrix\mbox{-}freedman}\) to both signs of this \((n+m)\)-dimensional martingale.  By (22)--(23), with \(R_{nm}=2B/q\),
\[
P\{\lVert E\rVert\ge t\}
\le2(n+m)\exp\!\left\{-\frac{t^2/2}{v_{nm}+R_{nm}t/3}\right\}.
\tag{24}
\]
The terminal dilation has operator norm \(\lVert E\rVert\).  Put \(L_{nm}=\log(2(n+m))\).  Direct substitution in (24) shows that, for every \(x\ge0\),
\[
P\!\left\{\lVert E\rVert>
\sqrt{2v_{nm}(L_{nm}+x)}+
\frac{2R_{nm}}3(L_{nm}+x)\right\}\le e^{-x}.
\tag{25}
\]
Indeed, for \(u=L_{nm}+x\) and \(t=\sqrt{2v_{nm}u}+2R_{nm}u/3\),
\[
t^2-2u(v_{nm}+R_{nm}t/3)
=\frac{2R_{nm}u}{3}\sqrt{2v_{nm}u}\ge0.
\]
Integrating (25), using \(\sqrt{L_{nm}+x}\le\sqrt{L_{nm}}+\sqrt x\), \(\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx=1\), and \(\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\sqrt x\,dx<\infty\), yields
\[
E_P\lVert E\rVert
\le CB\left\{
\sqrt{\frac{(n\vee m)\log(e(n+m))}{q}}+
\frac{\log(e(n+m))}{q}\right\}
=:C\eta_{nm}.
\tag{26}
\]
All constants through (26) are uniform in \(P\).

We now pass from operator error to the declared loss without any predictability premise on \(U\) or \(V\).  Let \(P_U=UU^\top\), and let \((\widehat U,\widehat\Sigma,\widehat V)\) be the leading rank-\(r\) singular triple of \(M+E\) under the fixed tie rule.  Exact rank gives \((I-P_U)M=0\).  On \(\{\lVert E\rVert<\lambda_{nm}/2\}\), the singular-value min--max formula and the signal floor give
\[
\sigma_r(\widehat\Sigma)\ge\sigma_r(M)-\lVert E\rVert
\ge\lambda_{nm}-\lVert E\rVert>0.
\]
Projecting \((M+E)\widehat V=\widehat U\widehat\Sigma\) onto the orthogonal complement of \(U\) yields
\[
\lVert(I-P_U)\widehat U\rVert
\le\frac{\lVert E\rVert}{\lambda_{nm}-\lVert E\rVert}
\le\frac{2\lVert E\rVert}{\lambda_{nm}}.
\tag{27}
\]
The singular-value decomposition of \(U^\top\widehat U\), together with \(2(1-\cos x)\le2\sin^2x\), supplies \(R\in\mathbb O_r\) such that
\[
\lVert\widehat UR-U\rVert
\le\sqrt2\lVert(I-P_U)\widehat U\rVert.
\tag{28}
\]
Off the event in (27), the left side of (28) is at most two.  Since \(\lVert Q\rVert_{2,\infty}\le\lVert Q\rVert\), the two cases imply
\[
\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm I},U)
\le C\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}
\left(1\wedge\frac{\lVert E\rVert}{\lambda_{nm}}\right).
\tag{29}
\]
The leading left singular vectors of \(\mathcal P_r(M+E)\) are those of \(M+E\) under the same fixed tie rule, so \(\widehat U=\widehat U^{\mathrm I}\).  The map \(x\mapsto1\wedge x\) is concave on \(\mathbb R_+\).  Jensen's inequality and (26)--(29) therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_P\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm I},U)
&\le C\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}
E_P\left[1\wedge\frac{\lVert E\rVert}{\lambda_{nm}}\right]\\
&\le C\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}
\left(1\wedge\frac{\eta_{nm}}{\lambda_{nm}}\right)
\le C a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the supremum over the declared class proves the proposition.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r}\) be the frame in \(\mathrm{def:deterministic\mbox{-}sine\mbox{-}frame}\).  Then
\[
S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r}\in\mathbb O_{n,r},\qquad
\lVert S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r}\rVert_{2,\infty}\le\sqrt{\frac{2r}{n+1}}.
\]
For every \(U\in\mathbb O_{n,r}\) satisfying \(\lVert U\rVert_{2,\infty}\le\sqrt{\mu r/n}\),
\[
\mathcal L(S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r},U)\le
1+\sqrt{\frac{2n}{\mu(n+1)}}\le1+\sqrt{\frac2\mu}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For \(1\le k\le2n\), the finite geometric-series identity, with \(x_k=\pi k/(n+1)\), gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\cos(ix_k)=
\frac{\sin(nx_k/2)\cos((n+1)x_k/2)}{\sin(x_k/2)}
=\begin{cases}0,&k\text{ is odd},\\-1,&k\text{ is even}.
\end{cases}
\tag{30}
\]
The denominator is nonzero because \(0<k<2(n+1)\).  The two displayed values follow respectively from \(\cos(k\pi/2)=0\) and, for even \(k=2h\),
\(\sin(h\pi-h\pi/(n+1))\cos(h\pi)=-\sin(h\pi/(n+1))\).

For \(1\le s,t\le r\), use \(2\sin x\sin y=\cos(x-y)-\cos(x+y)\).  If \(s\ne t\), the integers \(|s-t|\) and \(s+t\) have the same parity and lie between \(1\) and \(2n\); (30) makes the two cosine sums equal.  If \(s=t\), the first cosine sum is \(n\), while (30) makes the sum with index \(2s\) equal to \(-1\).  Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi is}{n+1}\right)
\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi it}{n+1}\right)
=\frac{n+1}{2}{\bf1}\{s=t\}.
\]
The normalization in \(\mathrm{def:deterministic\mbox{-}sine\mbox{-}frame}\) now proves \(S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r}\in\mathbb O_{n,r}\).  Since every squared sine is at most one,
\[
\max_i\lVert e_i^\top S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r}\rVert_2^2
=\max_i\frac2{n+1}\sum_{s=1}^r
\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi is}{n+1}\right)
\le\frac{2r}{n+1}.
\tag{31}
\]

For the loss, choose \(R=I_r\) in \(\mathrm{def:rowwise\mbox{-}loss}\), apply the rowwise triangle inequality, then use (31) and the stated incoherence bound:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L(S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r},U)
&\le\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}
\left(\lVert S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r}\rVert_{2,\infty}
+\lVert U\rVert_{2,\infty}\right)\\
&\le\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}
\left(\sqrt{\frac{2r}{n+1}}+\sqrt{\frac{\mu r}{n}}\right)\\
&=1+\sqrt{\frac{2n}{\mu(n+1)}}\le1+\sqrt{\frac2\mu}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves every assertion pathwise.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}\) and \(\widehat U^{\mathrm H}\) be defined by \(\mathrm{def:loose\mbox{-}spectral\mbox{-}radius}\) and \(\mathrm{def:hybrid\mbox{-}estimator}\).  For every \(n,m\ge2\), \(\widehat U^{\mathrm H}\in\mathfrak E_{n,m}\), and there is a universal constant \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}(r,\mu,K,q,B,\lambda)}
E_P[\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm H},U)]
\le C(1\wedge a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}).
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
The quantity \(a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}\) is deterministic for fixed class parameters.  The recorded score is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal O_{n,m}=\sigma(A,Y,p)\), and \(\widehat U^{\mathrm I}\) is an orthonormal random matrix obtained from it by the fixed rank projection and tie rule in \(\mathrm{def:ipw\mbox{-}svd}\).  The sine frame is deterministic and orthonormal by \(\mathrm{prop:deterministic\mbox{-}sine\mbox{-}fallback}\).  Hence both branches of \(\mathrm{def:hybrid\mbox{-}estimator}\) are \(\mathcal O_{n,m}\)-measurable and take values in \(\mathbb O_{n,r}\).  Thus \(\widehat U^{\mathrm H}\in\mathfrak E_{n,m}\) by \(\mathrm{def:observed\mbox{-}estimators}\).

If \(a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}\le1\), then \(\widehat U^{\mathrm H}=\widehat U^{\mathrm I}\), so \(\mathrm{prop:ipw\mbox{-}expected\mbox{-}risk\mbox{-}upper}\) gives
\[
\sup_P E_P[\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm H},U)]
\le C_{\mathrm I}a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}
=C_{\mathrm I}(1\wedge a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}).
\]
If \(a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}>1\), then \(\widehat U^{\mathrm H}=S^{\mathrm{sin}}_{n,r}\).  Every \(P\) in the predictable class satisfies the left-incoherence assumption.  Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:deterministic\mbox{-}sine\mbox{-}fallback}\) and \(\mu\ge1\) therefore imply pathwise
\[
\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm H},U)\le1+\sqrt{2/\mu}\le1+\sqrt2
\le(1+\sqrt2)(1\wedge a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}).
\]
Taking \(C=\max\{C_{\mathrm I},1+\sqrt2\}\) proves the bound in both cases.  No property beyond the frozen class was used.

added_lemmas.statement:
Fix \(r\), \(K\), and \(\mu>1\).  There are constants \(c_0,c_1,c,C>0\), depending only on these fixed quantities, \(q\), and the aspect bounds, such that, for all sufficiently large \(n,m\), whenever \(b_{nm}\le c_0\) and \(\lambda_{nm}\le c_1B\sqrt{nm}\),
\[
cb_{nm}\le
\inf_{\widetilde U\in\mathfrak E_{n,m}}
\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}(r,\mu,K,q,B,\lambda)}
E_P[\mathcal L(\widetilde U,U)]
\le
\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}(r,\mu,K,q,B,\lambda)}
E_P[\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm H},U)]
\le C(1\wedge a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}).
\]
Separately, recorded IPW--SVD obeys the generally looser bound
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}(r,\mu,K,q,B,\lambda)}
E_P[\mathcal L(\widehat U^{\mathrm I},U)]\le C a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}.
\]
The endogenous-target obstruction rules out uniform \(b_{nm}\)-attainment by this recorded IPW--SVD estimator, but it does not give an impossibility result for every member of \(\mathfrak E_{n,m}\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a sufficiently large pair \((n,m)\) for which the declared class is nonempty, and choose
\(P\in\mathfrak P^{\mathrm{pred}}_{n,m}(r,\mu,K,q,B,\lambda)\).  By the bounded-outcomes assumption incorporated in \(\mathrm{def:predictable\mbox{-}class}\), conditional expectation and the conditional triangle inequality give, for \(a\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
 |\mu^a_{ij}|
 =\left|E_P\!\left[Y_{ij}(a)\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}\right]\right|
 \le E_P\!\left[|Y_{ij}(a)|\mid\mathbb G_{o(i,j)-1}\right]
 \le B
\]
almost surely.  Hence the definition \(M=\mu^1-\mu^0\) yields
\[
 |M_{ij}|\le |\mu^1_{ij}|+|\mu^0_{ij}|\le 2B.
\]
Summing squares over the \(nm\) cells therefore gives
\[
 \lVert M\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2
 =\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^m M_{ij}^2
 \le 4B^2nm.
\]
For every matrix, the largest singular value is at most the Frobenius norm because
\(\lVert M\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2\) is the sum of the squared singular values.  The signal-floor assumption in \(\mathrm{def:predictable\mbox{-}class}\) consequently implies
\[
 \lambda_{nm}\le\sigma_r(M)\le\sigma_1(M)
 \le\lVert M\rVert_{\mathrm F}\le 2B\sqrt{nm}.
\]
This establishes the signal ceiling; its divisions below are valid because \(B>0\), \(q>0\), and \(\lambda_{nm}>0\).

Let
\[
 T_{nm}=\frac{B\sqrt{nm}}{\lambda_{nm}}\sqrt{\log(en)}\,b^0_{nm}
\]
be the untruncated expression defining \(b_{nm}\).  The signal ceiling and \(\sqrt{n^{-1}+nm^{-2}}\ge n^{-1/2}\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 T_{nm}
 &\ge \frac12\sqrt{\log(en)}\,
 K r^{3/2}\mu q^{-1/2}\sqrt{n^{-1}+nm^{-2}}\\
 &\ge \frac{K r^{3/2}\mu}{2\sqrt q}
 \sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}n}
 =:z_{b,n}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Because \(z_{b,n}\to0\), one has \(z_{b,n}\le1\) eventually.  Positivity and monotonicity of \(x\mapsto1\wedge x\) then yield
\[
 b_{nm}=1\wedge T_{nm}\ge1\wedge z_{b,n}=z_{b,n},
\]
which is the asserted floor for \(b_{nm}\).

Put \(N_{nm}=n\vee m\).  Since
\[
 \frac{N_{nm}}{nm}=\frac1{n\wedge m}\ge\frac1n
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \log(e(n+m))\ge\log(en),
\]
the signal ceiling gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 x^{a}_{nm}
 &:=\frac B{\lambda_{nm}}\left\{
 \sqrt{\frac{N_{nm}\log(e(n+m))}{q}}+
 \frac{\log(e(n+m))}{q}\right\}\\
 &\ge \frac1{2\sqrt{nm}}
 \sqrt{\frac{N_{nm}\log(e(n+m))}{q}}\\
 &\ge\frac1{2\sqrt q}\sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}n}
 =:z_{a,n}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The second summand in the definition of \(x^a_{nm}\) is nonnegative.  Since \(z_{a,n}\to0\), the same truncation argument gives
\[
 a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}
 =\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}\,(1\wedge x^a_{nm})
 \ge\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}\,z_{a,n}
 =\frac1{2\sqrt{\mu r q}}\sqrt{\log(en)}.
\]
Similarly, if
\[
 x^d_{nm}=\frac B{\lambda_{nm}}\left\{
 q^{-1}\sqrt{N_{nm}\log(e(n+m))}+q^{-3}\log(en)
 \right\},
\]
then nonnegativity of its second summand and the preceding two elementary comparisons imply
\[
 x^d_{nm}\ge\frac1{2q}\sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}n}=:z_{d,n}.
\]
Because \(z_{d,n}\to0\), it follows that
\[
 d_{nm}=\sqrt{\frac n{\mu r}}\,(1\wedge x^d_{nm})
 \ge\frac1{2q\sqrt{\mu r}}\sqrt{\log(en)}.
\]
The constants \(r,\mu,q\) are fixed and positive, while \(\log(en)\to\infty\); hence both \(a^{\mathrm{loose}}_{nm}\) and \(d_{nm}\) diverge.

It remains to verify the final conditional comparison.  Bounded aspect ratio gives
\[
 m\asymp n,\qquad n\vee m\asymp n,\qquad
 \log(e(n+m))\asymp\log(en),
\]
and therefore
\[
 \sqrt{nm}\sqrt{n^{-1}+nm^{-2}}\asymp\sqrt n.
\]
As \(r,\mu,K,q\) are fixed positive constants, these relations and the two rate definitions imply
\[
